title: The silkworm's house
hookLine: a silkworm spins its own house from inside itself, and is caught in it: Akka Mahadevi's picture of desire
carry: my wanting binds; the Lord's grace sets free
tomorrow: The test at the hall of saints
last: THE LORD IS PRESENT IN THE MURTI.

lines: HER NAME FOR GOD WAS A FLOWER.
cards: A silkworm doesn't find its house. It makes it, out of its own body, thread by thread, turning and turning, until the house is finished and the worm is sealed inside.
Everything it needed came from within it, and so did the trap. That small, exact picture opens one of the sayings of a woman people called Akka, elder sister.
She spoke to Shiva in Kannada, in the south, and her name for him was a flower.

teach.h: AKKA, ELDER SISTER, SAINT OF SHIVA
teach.b: Her name is Mahadevi, and people called her Akka, elder sister, so she comes down to us as Akka Mahadevi.

She belongs to the Virashaiva, or Lingayat, saints of Karnataka, devotees of Shiva who spoke their faith in short, sharp sayings called vachanas. They're closer to speech than hymns, in plain Kannada.
Her sayings carry her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna.
Some readers render it as the beautiful lord, white as jasmine: a god called by the name of a small white flower. The silkworm, in paraphrase.
The silkworm builds its house lovingly out of itself, and dies tangled in what it wound. So I burn with my heart's wanting. Lord white as jasmine, cut through this greed in me, and show me a way out.
Notice first: she doesn't blame the world for trapping her.
The thread comes from inside, her own wanting, spun round and round. That's an old Hindu teaching, said plainly: what binds us is our own desire. And notice second: she doesn't free herself.
She asks Shiva to cut the thread.

His devotees call that freeing gift his grace, anugraha, one of the five acts the tradition gives him. So the saying holds both halves of the faith at once: I spun this, and I need the Lord to free me.
Then listen to the voice. No priest stands between her and Shiva, no special language. A woman speaks in her own tongue to a god she calls by the name of a flower.

how: Lingayats and other devotees of Shiva in Karnataka honor Akka Mahadevi among the vachana saints; her sayings are recited, sung and taught, and are read in Kannada and in translation.

o: elder sister: a saint who spoke plainly to Shiva
a goddess of the silkworm and the weaver's thread
a queen who built Karnataka's great Shiva temples

p: Shiva's grace that sets the soul free
a short saying in plain Kannada
spins its own house, and is caught

s: in the silkworm saying, Akka blames the world for trapping her
the thread comes from inside, from her own wanting.
in the saying, Akka frees herself by trying harder
she asks Shiva to cut the thread; his devotees call that freeing gift his grace, anugraha.
vachanas are short sayings in plain Kannada, close to speech
not temple hymns in Sanskrit: a person talking straight to God.

games.q: you're Akka, caught in your own threads like the silkworm. how does the saying ask for a way out?
o: by trying harder to escape alone.
by asking the lord white as jasmine to cut through.
by blaming the people around her.
games.why: she asks him to cut through her heart's greed and show her the way out. the release, in the saying, is his doing.

practice: Notice one wanting active in you right now, a snack, a message, a result. Don't fight it or follow it; watch it spin like a silkworm turning. Devotees of Shiva often repeat his five-syllable mantra, namah shivaya.
If you pray, say it softly on each out-breath and ask him, as Akka did, to cut the thread. If you don't, loosen your grip a little with each breath out.
